claim: Neural crest development is transcriptionally controlled via sequential activation of gene regulatory networks (GRNs).
source: While neural crest development is known to be transcriptionally controlled via sequential activation of gene regulatory networks (GRNs), recent evidence increasingly implicates a role for post-transcriptional regulation in modulating the output of these regulatory circuits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation plays a role in modulating the output of neural crest gene regulatory circuits.
source: While neural crest development is known to be transcriptionally controlled via sequential activation of gene regulatory networks (GRNs), recent evidence increasingly implicates a role for post-transcriptional regulation in modulating the output of these regulatory circuits.
evidence: This is stated as recent evidence in the abstract.

claim: Elavl1 is enriched in the premigratory cranial neural crest.
source: Using available single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from avian embryos to identify potential post-transcriptional regulators, we found that Elavl1, which encodes for an RNA-binding protein with roles in transcript stability, was enriched in the premigratory cranial neural crest.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elavl1 encodes an RNA-binding protein with roles in transcript stability.
source: Using available single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from avian embryos to identify potential post-transcriptional regulators, we found that Elavl1, which encodes for an RNA-binding protein with roles in transcript stability, was enriched in the premigratory cranial neural crest.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Elavl1 function.

claim: Perturbation of Elavl1 results in premature neural crest delamination from the neural tube.
source: Perturbation of Elavl1 resulted in premature neural crest delamination from the neural tube as well as significant reduction in transcripts associated with the neural crest specification GRN, phenotypes that are also observed with downregulation of the canonical Wnt inhibitor Draxin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Perturbation of Elavl1 results in significant reduction in transcripts associated with the neural crest specification GRN.
source: Perturbation of Elavl1 resulted in premature neural crest delamination from the neural tube as well as significant reduction in transcripts associated with the neural crest specification GRN, phenotypes that are also observed with downregulation of the canonical Wnt inhibitor Draxin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Downregulation of Draxin results in premature neural crest delamination and reduction in neural crest specification transcripts.
source: Perturbation of Elavl1 resulted in premature neural crest delamination from the neural tube as well as significant reduction in transcripts associated with the neural crest specification GRN, phenotypes that are also observed with downregulation of the canonical Wnt inhibitor Draxin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Draxin is a canonical Wnt inhibitor.
source: Perturbation of Elavl1 resulted in premature neural crest delamination from the neural tube as well as significant reduction in transcripts associated with the neural crest specification GRN, phenotypes that are also observed with downregulation of the canonical Wnt inhibitor Draxin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Draxin function.

claim: Draxin is the primary target for stabilization by Elavl1 during cranial neural crest specification.
source: That Draxin is the primary target for stabilization by Elavl1 during cranial neural crest specification was shown by RNA-sequencing, RNA immunoprecipitation, RNA decay measurement, and proximity ligation assays, further supporting the idea that the downregulation of neural crest specifier expression upon Elavl1 knockdown was largely due to loss of Draxin.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including RNA-seq, RIP, RNA decay assays, and PLA.

claim: Downregulation of neural crest specifier expression upon Elavl1 knockdown is largely due to loss of Draxin.
source: That Draxin is the primary target for stabilization by Elavl1 during cranial neural crest specification was shown by RNA-sequencing, RNA immunoprecipitation, RNA decay measurement, and proximity ligation assays, further supporting the idea that the downregulation of neural crest specifier expression upon Elavl1 knockdown was largely due to loss of Draxin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and inference from multiple assays.

claim: Exogenous Draxin rescues cranial neural crest specification defects observed with Elavl1 knockdown.
source: Importantly, exogenous Draxin rescued cranial neural crest specification defects observed with Elavl1 knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elavl1 plays a critical role in the maintenance of cranial neural crest specification via Draxin mRNA stabilization.
source: Thus, Elavl1 plays a critical a role in the maintenance of cranial neural crest specification via Draxin mRNA stabilization.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation intersects with modulation of the neural crest specification GRN.
source: Together, these data highlight an important intersection of post-transcriptional regulation with modulation of the neural crest specification GRN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Neural crest cells undergo coordinated induction, specification, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) events to migrate and form various tissues.
source: During development, these cells undergo coordinated induction, specification, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) events to migrate and ultimately form a myriad of tissues, including craniofacial structures, components of the peripheral nervous system, as well as many other derivatives (Gandhi and Bronner, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Neural crest cells form craniofacial structures, components of the peripheral nervous system, and many other derivatives.
source: During development, these cells undergo coordinated induction, specification, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) events to migrate and ultimately form a myriad of tissues, including craniofacial structures, components of the peripheral nervous system, as well as many other derivatives (Gandhi and Bronner, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The transcriptional control of neural crest development has been dissected and mapped into modules of a feed-forward gene regulatory network.
source: The transcriptional control of these events has been dissected and mapped into modules of a feed-forward gene regulatory network (GRN), which helps explain the detailed sequence of events involved in neural crest development (Martik and Bronner, 2017; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015a; Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: There is growing appreciation for the role that post-transcriptional regulation plays in neural crest formation.
source: Recently, in addition to transcriptional events, there has been growing appreciation for the role that post-transcriptional regulation plays in the establishment, maintenance, and regulation of neural crest formation (Bhattacharya et al., 2018; Cibi et al., 2019; Copeland and Simoes-Costa, 2020; Forman et al., 2021; Sánchez-Vásquez et al., 2019; Ward et al., 2018; Weiner, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as recent evidence with multiple citations.

claim: RNA-binding proteins play an essential role in post-transcriptional regulatory processes.
source: Given that RNA-binding proteins play an essential role in post-transcriptional regulatory processes (Dassi, 2017), we sought to broadly identify those with early roles in neural crest development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Elavl1 is a nucleocytoplasmic shuttling protein from the ELAV (embryonic lethal abnormal vision) family of RNA-binding proteins.
source: Elavl1 is a nucleocytoplasmic shuttling protein from the ELAV (embryonic lethal abnormal vision) family of RNA-binding proteins, which have conserved roles in neural development (Ma et al., 1996; Yao et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The ELAV family of RNA-binding proteins has conserved roles in neural development.
source: Elavl1 is a nucleocytoplasmic shuttling protein from the ELAV (embryonic lethal abnormal vision) family of RNA-binding proteins, which have conserved roles in neural development (Ma et al., 1996; Yao et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Elavl1 is a well-established stabilizer of mRNA.
source: It is a well-established stabilizer of mRNA, a function often mediated via association with the 3′-untranslated region (3′-UTR) of its mRNA targets (Abdelmohsen and Gorospe, 2010; Rothamel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Elavl1's mRNA stabilization function is often mediated via association with the 3′-untranslated region (3′-UTR) of its mRNA targets.
source: It is a well-established stabilizer of mRNA, a function often mediated via association with the 3′-untranslated region (3′-UTR) of its mRNA targets (Abdelmohsen and Gorospe, 2010; Rothamel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Elavl1 is essential for mammalian development and embryonic survival.
source: Elavl1 is essential for mammalian development and embryonic survival; Elavl1 null mouse embryos exhibit lethality due to abnormal placental morphogenesis, and conditional epiblast-null embryos display a broad array of phenotypes, ranging from defects in ossification and craniofacial development to asplenia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from mouse studies.

claim: Elavl1 null mouse embryos exhibit lethality due to abnormal placental morphogenesis.
source: Elavl1 is essential for mammalian development and embryonic survival; Elavl1 null mouse embryos exhibit lethality due to abnormal placental morphogenesis, and conditional epiblast-null embryos display a broad array of phenotypes, ranging from defects in ossification and craniofacial development to asplenia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from mouse studies.

claim: Conditional epiblast-null Elavl1 mouse embryos display defects in ossification and craniofacial development.
source: Elavl1 is essential for mammalian development and embryonic survival; Elavl1 null mouse embryos exhibit lethality due to abnormal placental morphogenesis, and conditional epiblast-null embryos display a broad array of phenotypes, ranging from defects in ossification and craniofacial development to asplenia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from mouse studies.

claim: Elavl1 acts on specific gene networks in a spatiotemporally controlled manner during embryonic development.
source: Interestingly, despite the myriad of tissue systems affected by Elavl1 knockout and relatively broad expression in wild-type embryos, mechanistic insights suggest Elavl1 acts on specific gene networks in a spatiotemporally controlled manner (Katsanou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Perturbation of Elavl1 led to premature neural crest delamination.
source: The results show that perturbation of Elavl1 led to premature neural crest delamination, as well as significant reduction in the expression of genes within the neural crest specification GRN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Perturbation of Elavl1 led to significant reduction in the expression of genes within the neural crest specification GRN.
source: The results show that perturbation of Elavl1 led to premature neural crest delamination, as well as significant reduction in the expression of genes within the neural crest specification GRN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The effects of Elavl1 perturbation were mediated by loss of Draxin.
source: We find that these effects were mediated by loss of Draxin, a direct mRNA target for stabilization by Elavl1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and rescue experiments.

claim: Draxin is a direct mRNA target for stabilization by Elavl1.
source: We find that these effects were mediated by loss of Draxin, a direct mRNA target for stabilization by Elavl1.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including RIP, RNA decay assays, and PLA.

claim: Elavl1 plays a critical role in the regulation of a critical neural crest specification module.
source: Our data demonstrate a critical role for Elavl1, and RNA-binding protein-mediated post-transcriptional control, in the regulation of a critical neural crest specification module.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data.

claim: RNA-binding protein-mediated post-transcriptional control plays a critical role in the regulation of a neural crest specification module.
source: Our data demonstrate a critical role for Elavl1, and RNA-binding protein-mediated post-transcriptional control, in the regulation of a critical neural crest specification module.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data.

claim: Three distinct clusters (neural, premigratory, and delaminating/migratory) were identified among cranial neural crest cells isolated from avian embryos at the 5–6 somite stage.
source: To identify RNA-binding proteins with potential roles in cranial neural crest specification, we analyzed scRNA-seq data for cranial neural crest isolated from avian embryos at the 5–6 somite stage (Williams et al., 2019) we identified three distinct clusters (neural, premigratory [pNC], and delaminating/migratory [mNC]) among which genes associated with the gene ontology (GO) term 'binds to 3′-UTR' were differentially expressed (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of scRNA-seq data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Genes associated with the gene ontology term 'binds to 3′-UTR' were differentially expressed among neural, premigratory, and delaminating/migratory neural crest clusters.
source: To identify RNA-binding proteins with potential roles in cranial neural crest specification, we analyzed scRNA-seq data for cranial neural crest isolated from avian embryos at the 5–6 somite stage (Williams et al., 2019) we identified three distinct clusters (neural, premigratory [pNC], and delaminating/migratory [mNC]) among which genes associated with the gene ontology (GO) term 'binds to 3′-UTR' were differentially expressed (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Elavl1 was the only gene associated with all three GO terms 'stabilizes RNA', 'regulates translation', and 'binds to 3′-UTR' that was abundantly expressed in isolated cranial neural crest cells.
source: To isolate potential positive regulators of neural crest specification, we then performed GO term analysis for 'stabilizes RNA' and 'regulates translation' among the identified RNA-binding proteins; only the Elavl1 gene was associated with all three GO terms and abundantly expressed in the isolated cranial neural crest cells (Figure 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 1F, G.

claim: Elavl1 knockout mice often display defects in craniofacial structures.
source: Given that Elavl1 knockout mice often display defects in craniofacial structures (Katsanou et al., 2009), and the transcript appeared enriched in premigratory cranial neural crest cells (Figure 1E), we hypothesized a potential role for Elavl1 during cranial neural crest specification.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: At HH8−, Elavl1 expression was detected in the anterior open neural tube and closing neural folds surrounding the anterior neuropore but absent from Pax7-expressing NPB cells.
source: Early in neurulation, when the neural plate border (NPB) is established within the rising neural folds, Elavl1 expression was detected in the anterior open neural tube and closing neural folds surrounding the anterior neuropore but absent from Pax7-expressing NPB cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: As the neural tube closed, Elavl1 expression became enriched throughout the neural tube and overlapped with Pax7 expression in premigratory cranial neural crest cells.
source: As the neural tube closed, when neural crest specification is complete, Elavl1 expression became enriched throughout the neural tube and overlapped with Pax7 expression in premigratory cranial neural crest cells (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Following cranial neural crest EMT, Elavl1 remained expressed in the migratory neural crest cells, as well as throughout the brain and neural tube.
source: Following cranial neural crest EMT, Elavl1 remained expressed in the migratory neural crest cells, as well as throughout the brain and neural tube (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Elavl1 is expressed in specified, premigratory cranial neural crest cells following establishment of the NPB.
source: Thus, Elavl1 is expressed in specified, premigratory cranial neural crest cells following establishment of the NPB and is retained during the onset of EMT and in early migrating cranial neural crest cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the expression pattern data.

claim: Elavl1 is retained during the onset of EMT and in early migrating cranial neural crest cells.
source: Thus, Elavl1 is expressed in specified, premigratory cranial neural crest cells following establishment of the NPB and is retained during the onset of EMT and in early migrating cranial neural crest cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the expression pattern data.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown resulted in 61.4 ± 0.9% of control side Elavl1 expression (p < 0.001).
source: Following Elavl1 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; 61.4 ± 0.9% of the control side, p < 0.001, paired t-test, n = 5 embryos, 15 sections), we observed significant reduction in the levels of Axud1 (Figure 3C; 73.7 ± 3.1% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos), FoxD3 (Figure 3D; 61.3 ± 5.5% of the control side, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 10 embryos), and Draxin (Figure 3E; 66.6 ± 1.8% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos) transcripts compared to contralateral control sides.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown resulted in significant reduction in Axud1 transcript levels (73.7 ± 3.1% of control side, p = 0.03).
source: Following Elavl1 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; 61.4 ± 0.9% of the control side, p < 0.001, paired t-test, n = 5 embryos, 15 sections), we observed significant reduction in the levels of Axud1 (Figure 3C; 73.7 ± 3.1% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos), FoxD3 (Figure 3D; 61.3 ± 5.5% of the control side, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 10 embryos), and Draxin (Figure 3E; 66.6 ± 1.8% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos) transcripts compared to contralateral control sides.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative HCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown resulted in significant reduction in FoxD3 transcript levels (61.3 ± 5.5% of control side, p = 0.002).
source: Following Elavl1 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; 61.4 ± 0.9% of the control side, p < 0.001, paired t-test, n = 5 embryos, 15 sections), we observed significant reduction in the levels of Axud1 (Figure 3C; 73.7 ± 3.1% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos), FoxD3 (Figure 3D; 61.3 ± 5.5% of the control side, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 10 embryos), and Draxin (Figure 3E; 66.6 ± 1.8% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos) transcripts compared to contralateral control sides.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative HCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown resulted in significant reduction in Draxin transcript levels (66.6 ± 1.8% of control side, p = 0.03).
source: Following Elavl1 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; 61.4 ± 0.9% of the control side, p < 0.001, paired t-test, n = 5 embryos, 15 sections), we observed significant reduction in the levels of Axud1 (Figure 3C; 73.7 ± 3.1% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos), FoxD3 (Figure 3D; 61.3 ± 5.5% of the control side, p = 0.002, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 10 embryos), and Draxin (Figure 3E; 66.6 ± 1.8% of the control side, p = 0.03, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 6 embryos) transcripts compared to contralateral control sides.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative HCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown did not significantly affect Pax7 expression (87.4 ± 3.1% of control side, p = 0.1).
source: To parse whether this was a specific effect or a broad defect in neural crest development, we also examined additional neural crest genes and found no significant difference in expression between control or Elavl1 knockdown sides for Pax7 (Figure 3F; 87.4 ± 3.1% of the control side, p = 0.1, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 5 embryos) or Tfap2b (Figure 3G; 98.2 ± 7.0% of the control side, p = 0.6, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 4 embryos), indicating a specific defect in a subset of genes required for cranial neural crest specification.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative HCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown did not significantly affect Tfap2b expression (98.2 ± 7.0% of control side, p = 0.6).
source: To parse whether this was a specific effect or a broad defect in neural crest development, we also examined additional neural crest genes and found no significant difference in expression between control or Elavl1 knockdown sides for Pax7 (Figure 3F; 87.4 ± 3.1% of the control side, p = 0.1, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 5 embryos) or Tfap2b (Figure 3G; 98.2 ± 7.0% of the control side, p = 0.6, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 4 embryos), indicating a specific defect in a subset of genes required for cranial neural crest specification.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative HCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown causes a specific defect in a subset of genes required for cranial neural crest specification.
source: To parse whether this was a specific effect or a broad defect in neural crest development, we also examined additional neural crest genes and found no significant difference in expression between control or Elavl1 knockdown sides for Pax7 (Figure 3F; 87.4 ± 3.1% of the control side, p = 0.1, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 5 embryos) or Tfap2b (Figure 3G; 98.2 ± 7.0% of the control side, p = 0.6, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 4 embryos), indicating a specific defect in a subset of genes required for cranial neural crest specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on different neural crest genes.

claim: The total number of Pax7+ cells was unaffected with Elavl1 knockdown (101.3 ± 4.5% of control side, p = 0.6).
source: Interestingly, the total number of Pax7 + cells was unaffected with Elavl1 knockdown (101.3 ± 4.5% of the control side, p = 0.6, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 4 embryos, 11 sections); however, we found a significant increase in the number of Pax7 + cells that delaminated from the neural tube (139.4 ± 8.4% of the control side, p = 0.002, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test), and concomitant decrease in the number of Pax7 + cells retained within the dorsal neural tube (66.0 ± 5.3% of the control side, p = 0.001, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Figure 3H, I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown resulted in a significant increase in the number of Pax7+ cells that delaminated from the neural tube (139.4 ± 8.4% of control side, p = 0.002).
source: Interestingly, the total number of Pax7 + cells was unaffected with Elavl1 knockdown (101.3 ± 4.5% of the control side, p = 0.6, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 4 embryos, 11 sections); however, we found a significant increase in the number of Pax7 + cells that delaminated from the neural tube (139.4 ± 8.4% of the control side, p = 0.002, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test), and concomitant decrease in the number of Pax7 + cells retained within the dorsal neural tube (66.0 ± 5.3% of the control side, p = 0.001, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Figure 3H, I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown resulted in a concomitant decrease in the number of Pax7+ cells retained within the dorsal neural tube (66.0 ± 5.3% of control side, p = 0.001).
source: Interestingly, the total number of Pax7 + cells was unaffected with Elavl1 knockdown (101.3 ± 4.5% of the control side, p = 0.6, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 4 embryos, 11 sections); however, we found a significant increase in the number of Pax7 + cells that delaminated from the neural tube (139.4 ± 8.4% of the control side, p = 0.002, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test), and concomitant decrease in the number of Pax7 + cells retained within the dorsal neural tube (66.0 ± 5.3% of the control side, p = 0.001, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Figure 3H, I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: Elavl1 knockdown resulted in significant decrease in cranial neural crest emigration away from the midline (63.6 ± 4.1% of control side, p < 0.001).
source: To determine what impact premature delamination might have on cranial neural crest migration, we also performed whole mount immunostaining for Pax7 at HH9 + and found significant decrease in cranial neural crest emigration away from the midline (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; 63.6 ± 4.1% of the control side, p < 0.001, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test, n = 5 embryos, 5 measurements per embryo averaged).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elavl1 is required during early cranial neural crest development to regulate specification and prevent premature delamination.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Elavl1 is required during early cranial neural crest development to regulate specification and prevent premature delamination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Elavl1 knockdown effects.

claim: Among differentially expressed genes identified by RNA-seq, 12 were significantly downregulated with Elavl1 knockdown.
source: Among the differentially expressed genes we identified (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), 12 were significantly downregulated, with four having established roles in neural crest development and which we validated using HCR—Axud1, Draxin, BMP4, and Msx1 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four downregulated genes (Axud1, Draxin, BMP4, and Msx1) have established roles in neural crest development.
source: Among the differentially expressed genes we identified (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), 12 were significantly downregulated, with four having established roles in neural crest development and which we validated using HCR—Axud1, Draxin, BMP4, and Msx1 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and validated by HCR.

claim: Several canonical neural crest genes (Pax7, Tfap2b, Snai2, Sox9, and Zeb2) were unaffected with Elavl1 knockdown.
source: We also identified several canonical neural crest genes that were unaffected with Elavl1 knockdown (e.g., Pax7, Tfap2b, Snai2, Sox9, and Zeb2), consistent with HCR data (Figure 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elavl1 does not broadly bind and stabilize the transcripts of neural crest genes, rather it targets specific RNAs to drive cranial neural crest specification.
source: Together these data suggest Elavl1 does not broadly bind and stabilize the transcripts of neural crest genes, rather it targets specific RNAs to drive cranial neural crest specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effects on different neural crest genes.

claim: FoxD3 failed to meet stringency cutoff during RNA-seq analysis due to low expression at the examined stages.
source: Notably, FoxD3 failed to meet our stringency cutoff during RNA-seq analysis due to low expression at the examined stages, and is likely downregulated with Elavl1 knockdown (Figure 3D) due to indirect effects from loss of Axud1 (Simões-Costa et al., 2015b) and therefore unlikely to be a bona fide target of Elavl1.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why FoxD3 was not identified in RNA-seq.

claim: FoxD3 is likely downregulated with Elavl1 knockdown due to indirect effects from loss of Axud1.
source: Notably, FoxD3 failed to meet our stringency cutoff during RNA-seq analysis due to low expression at the examined stages, and is likely downregulated with Elavl1 knockdown (Figure 3D) due to indirect effects from loss of Axud1 (Simões-Costa et al., 2015b) and therefore unlikely to be a bona fide target of Elavl1.
evidence: This is inferred from the known relationship between Axud1 and FoxD3 with citation.

claim: FoxD3 is unlikely to be a bona fide target of Elavl1.
source: Notably, FoxD3 failed to meet our stringency cutoff during RNA-seq analysis due to low expression at the examined stages, and is likely downregulated with Elavl1 knockdown (Figure 3D) due to indirect effects from loss of Axud1 (Simões-Costa et al., 2015b) and therefore unlikely to be a bona fide target of Elavl1.
evidence: This is inferred from the indirect mechanism of FoxD3 downregulation.

claim: Among all transcripts tested (Draxin, Axud1, BMP4, Msx1, Pax7), only Draxin had a significant reduction in transcript stability with Elavl1 knockdown (p = 0.001).
source: Interestingly, among all the transcripts tested, only Draxin had a significant reduction in transcript stability (p = 0.001, Mann–Whitney test; Figure 4D), suggesting that Draxin is the primary target bound and stabilized by Elavl1 during cranial neural crest specification.
evidence: This is supported by RNA decay assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Draxin is the primary target bound and stabilized by Elavl1 during cranial neural crest specification.
source: Interestingly, among all the transcripts tested, only Draxin had a significant reduction in transcript stability (p = 0.001, Mann–Whitney test; Figure 4D), suggesting that Draxin is the primary target bound and stabilized by Elavl1 during cranial neural crest specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA decay assay results.

claim: The Draxin 3′-UTR contains four high probability Elavl1-binding sites.
source: The Draxin 3′-UTR contained four high probability-binding sites, whereas the other 3′-UTRs contained only one (BMP4, Msx1) or none (Axud1, Pax7, Tfap2b; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: BMP4 and Msx1 3′-UTRs contain only one high probability Elavl1-binding site.
source: The Draxin 3′-UTR contained four high probability-binding sites, whereas the other 3′-UTRs contained only one (BMP4, Msx1) or none (Axud1, Pax7, Tfap2b; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Axud1, Pax7, and Tfap2b 3′-UTRs contain no high probability Elavl1-binding sites.
source: The Draxin 3′-UTR contained four high probability-binding sites, whereas the other 3′-UTRs contained only one (BMP4, Msx1) or none (Axud1, Pax7, Tfap2b; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elavl1 contains three RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) that cooperate for RNA recognition.
source: Given that Elavl1 contains three RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) that cooperate for RNA recognition (Pabis et al., 2019), it is possible that multiple contacts are required for Elavl1 to bind and stabilize RNAs in vivo, and by extension is unlikely for Elavl1 to bind RNAs with only a single putative binding site.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Multiple contacts are required for Elavl1 to bind and stabilize RNAs in vivo.
source: Given that Elavl1 contains three RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) that cooperate for RNA recognition (Pabis et al., 2019), it is possible that multiple contacts are required for Elavl1 to bind and stabilize RNAs in vivo, and by extension is unlikely for Elavl1 to bind RNAs with only a single putative binding site.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known structure of Elavl1.

claim: Elavl1 is unlikely to bind RNAs with only a single putative binding site.
source: Given that Elavl1 contains three RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) that cooperate for RNA recognition (Pabis et al., 2019), it is possible that multiple contacts are required for Elavl1 to bind and stabilize RNAs in vivo, and by extension is unlikely for Elavl1 to bind RNAs with only a single putative binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for multiple contacts.

claim: Elavl1 specifically targets and stabilizes Draxin in cranial neural crest through multiple contact sites within its 3′-UTR.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that Elavl1 specifically targets and stabilizes Draxin in cranial neural crest through multiple contact sites within its 3′-UTR.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the binding site analysis and RNA decay data.

claim: Draxin mRNA was significantly enriched with Elavl1 IP compared to Pax7 and FoxD3 (p < 0.001).
source: We found that Pax7 and FoxD3 mRNAs (nontargets) were neither enriched in the IP, nor significantly different from each other (p = 0.89, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's post hoc test); however, Draxin mRNA was significantly enriched with Elavl1 IP compared to Pax7 and FoxD3 (p < 0.001, one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test; Figure 4F), suggesting that Elavl1 specifically associated with endogenous Draxin mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by RIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Elavl1 specifically associates with endogenous Draxin mRNA.

claim: Significantly more PLA puncta were observed with expression of MS2-Draxin 3′-UTR compared to control, indicating a specific and direct interaction between Elavl1 and the Draxin 3′-UTR.
source: We observed significantly more PLA puncta with expression of MS2-Draxin 3′-UTR (Figure 4H–I), indicating a specific and direct interaction between Elavl1 and the Draxin 3′-UTR.
evidence: This is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: Draxin knockdown resulted in significant reduction in FoxD3 transcript levels (26.8 ± 3.2% of control side, p < 0.02).
source: As with Elavl1 MO (Figure 3), we observed significant reduction in the levels of FoxD3 (Figure 5A; 26.8 ± 3.2% of the control side, p < 0.02, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank, n = 7 embryos), Axud1 (Figure 5B; 48.8 ± 5.1% of the control side, p < 0.01, paired t-test, n = 7 embryos), Msx1 (Figure 5C; 49.7 ± 5.8% of the control side, p < 0.01, paired t-test, n = 4 embryos), and BMP4 (Figure 5D; 63.6 ± 4.0% of the control side, p < 0.01, paired t-test, n = 4 embryos) transcripts compared to contralateral control sides (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by HCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Exogenous Draxin was sufficient to significantly restore FoxD3 expression from Elavl1 knockdown (84.5 ± 9.6% of control side, p < 0.05).
source: Indeed, exogenous Draxin was sufficient to significantly restore FoxD3 (Figure 5F; 84.5 ± 9.6% of the control side, n = 6 embryos), Axud1 (Figure 5G; 90.3 ± 5.0% of the control side, n = 6 embryos), Msx1 (Figure 5H; 91.0 ± 1.5% of the control side, n = 5 embryos), and BMP4 (Figure 5I; 96.5 ± 3.1% of the control side, n = 5 embryos) expression from Elavl1 knockdown (p < 0.05, one-tailed paired t-test) to expression levels not significantly different from control (Figure 5J; p > 0.09, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Co-electroporation of Draxin-FLAG with Elavl1 MO rescued the number of Pax7+ cells that delaminated and remained within the dorsal neural tube to near-control levels (91.6 ± 4.0% and 105.8 ± 12.0% of control side, respectively, p > 0.12).
source: Indeed, co-electroporation of Draxin-FLAG with Elavl1 MO was able to rescue the number of Pax7 + cells that delaminated and remained within the dorsal neural tube to near-control levels (Figure 5L; 91.6 ± 4.0% and 105.8 ± 12.0% of the control side, respectively, n = 3 embryos, 6 sections, p > 0.12, one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5K, L.

claim: Draxin mRNA is the primary target of Elavl1 in premigratory cranial neural crest.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that Draxin mRNA is the primary target of Elavl1 in premigratory cranial neural crest and is stabilized via 3′-UTR interaction to maintain neural crest specification.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from all the experimental data.

claim: Draxin is stabilized by Elavl1 via 3′-UTR interaction to maintain neural crest specification.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that Draxin mRNA is the primary target of Elavl1 in premigratory cranial neural crest and is stabilized via 3′-UTR interaction to maintain neural crest specification.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from all the experimental data.

claim: Loss of Elavl1 and Draxin interferes with output from multiple nodes of the GRNs required for neural crest specification, including those driven by Wnt and BMP.
source: We found that loss of Elavl1, and by extension its target, Draxin, interferes with output from multiple nodes of the GRNs required for neural crest specification, including those driven by Wnt and BMP (Hovland et al., 2020; Simões-Costa et al., 2015b; Tribulo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with citations.

claim: Elavl1 is a point of integration to coordinate signaling from parallel but independent GRNs.
source: Together, our data implicate Elavl1 as a point of integration to coordinate signaling from parallel but independent GRNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The study is consistent with previous work examining Elavl1 function in other cellular contexts with respect to its role as a stabilizing RNA-binding protein via 3′-UTR interaction.
source: At a mechanistic level, our study is consistent with previous work examining Elavl1 function in other cellular contexts, with respect to its role as a stabilizing RNA-binding protein via 3′-UTR interaction (Chen et al., 2002; Dormoy-Raclet et al., 2007; Katsanou et al., 2009; Rothamel et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as consistency with prior literature with citations.

claim: Prior work on Elavl1 knockout mice observed indirect downregulation of BMP4 with loss of Elavl1, though an upstream mediator remained unidentified.
source: In the context of embryonic development, our study aligns well with data from knockout mouse consistent with an important role for Elavl1 in intersecting signaling cascades; interestingly, this prior work similarly observed indirect downregulation of BMP4 with loss of Elavl1, though an upstream mediator remained unidentified (Katsanou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: Prior high-throughput studies found many RNAs directly bound by Elavl1.
source: In neural crest specification, we identified a single biologically relevant target of Elavl1, whereas prior high-throughput studies found many RNAs directly bound by Elavl1 (Mukherjee et al., 2011; Rothamel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: During embryonic development, Elavl1 function and RNA targets are driven by spatiotemporal determinants.
source: Whether this is a feature specific to neural crest is unclear, though the knockout mouse work suggests that during embryonic development Elavl1 function and RNA targets are driven by spatiotemporal determinants (Katsanou et al., 2009), which may be due RNP complex heterogeneity as a result of tissue-specific expression of other interacting RNA-binding proteins.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: Specificity of Elavl1 function in neural crest may be achieved through spatiotemporally regulated combinatorial expression of post-transcriptional regulators and RNA regulons.
source: Taken in the context of these prior studies, we speculate that despite broad tissue expression of Elavl1 across embryonic development, specificity in neural crest is achieved through spatiotemporally regulated combinatorial expression of post-transcriptional regulators and RNA regulons (Keene, 2007; Keene and Tenenbaum, 2002).
evidence: This is speculation based on prior literature with citations.

claim: Draxin must be rapidly downregulated for cranial neural crest EMT and migration to proceed.
source: It is important to note that, while Elavl1 expression persists in cranial neural crest during the initiation of EMT and migration, Draxin must be rapidly downregulated for these processes to proceed (Hutchins and Bronner, 2018; Hutchins and Bronner, 2019; Hutchins et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Elavl1 becomes endogenously displaced from Draxin at the onset of EMT.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that Elavl1 becomes endogenously displaced from Draxin at the onset of EMT, though it is yet unclear how this is achieved.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the expression patterns and known requirements.

claim: RNA-binding proteins can alter association with targets due to post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation or alternative RNA-binding protein competition.
source: RNA-binding proteins are known to alter association with targets due to post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation or alternative RNA-binding protein competition (Dassi, 2017; García-Mauriño et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Inhibition of serine–threonine kinases in neural crest increases cell–cell adhesions and negatively impacts cell migration.
source: Indeed, inhibition of serine–threonine kinases has been shown in neural crest to increase cell–cell adhesions and negatively impact cell migration (Monier-Gavelle and Duband, 1995), suggesting kinase-driven signaling pathway activation coincident with neural crest EMT; this is interesting given established roles for serine–threonine phosphorylation in modulating Elavl1-RNA-binding activity and target selection (Grammatikakis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: Serine–threonine phosphorylation plays established roles in modulating Elavl1-RNA-binding activity and target selection.
source: Indeed, inhibition of serine–threonine kinases has been shown in neural crest to increase cell–cell adhesions and negatively impact cell migration (Monier-Gavelle and Duband, 1995), suggesting kinase-driven signaling pathway activation coincident with neural crest EMT; this is interesting given established roles for serine–threonine phosphorylation in modulating Elavl1-RNA-binding activity and target selection (Grammatikakis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Elavl1 serine–threonine phosphorylation, either in combination with or as an alternative to competitive RNA-binding protein displacement, likely facilitates Draxin release and turnover at the onset of EMT.
source: Thus, we speculate that Elavl1 serine–threonine phosphorylation, either in combination with or as an alternative to competitive RNA-binding protein displacement, likely facilitates Draxin release and turnover at the onset of EMT.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known mechanisms and expression patterns.

claim: There are likely additional targets and roles for Elavl1 beyond Draxin stabilization during neural crest development.
source: Because its primary target during specification is downregulated while Elavl1 expression persists, this suggests there are likely additional targets and roles for Elavl1 beyond Draxin stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistent expression of Elavl1 after Draxin downregulation.

claim: Elavl1 has been shown in other contexts to stabilize Snail1 and matrix metalloprotease-9 (MMP-9).
source: Elavl1 has been shown in other contexts to stabilize Snail1 (Dong et al., 2007) and matrix metalloprotease-9 (MMP-9) (Yuan et al., 2011), factors with well-established roles in neural crest EMT (Cano et al., 2000; Kalev-Altman et al., 2020; Monsonego-Ornan et al., 2012; Strobl-Mazzulla and Bronner, 2012; Taneyhill et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Snail1 and MMP-9 have well-established roles in neural crest EMT.
source: Elavl1 has been shown in other contexts to stabilize Snail1 (Dong et al., 2007) and matrix metalloprotease-9 (MMP-9) (Yuan et al., 2011), factors with well-established roles in neural crest EMT (Cano et al., 2000; Kalev-Altman et al., 2020; Monsonego-Ornan et al., 2012; Strobl-Mazzulla and Bronner, 2012; Taneyhill et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Elavl1 likely intersects with additional GRNs following neural crest specification.
source: Given that the neural crest specification GRNs is proceeded by activation of an EMT GRN also coinciding with Elavl1 expression, we speculate that Elavl1 likely intersects with additional GRNs following specification.
evidence: This is speculation based on the expression pattern and known GRN progression.

claim: One or more of the downregulated genes identified through RNA-seq that were not important for specification may yet be targets of Elavl1 with functions later in neural crest development.
source: It is possible one or more of the downregulated genes we identified through RNA-seq that were not important for specification may yet be targets of Elavl1, with functions later in neural crest development.
evidence: This is speculation about potential additional targets.

claim: Cranial neural crest cells are indispensable for proper craniofacial development.
source: Cranial neural crest cells are indispensable for proper craniofacial development (van Limborgh et al., 1983; Vega-Lopez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Transcription factors have been well-established as critical regulators of neural crest development and craniofacial morphogenesis.
source: Whereas transcription factors have been well-established critical regulators of neural crest development and craniofacial morphogenesis reviewed in Gou et al., 2015, growing evidence indicates an essential role for post-transcriptional regulation in these processes (Cibi et al., 2019; Copeland and Simoes-Costa, 2020; Dennison et al., 2021; Forman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Growing evidence indicates an essential role for post-transcriptional regulation in neural crest development and craniofacial morphogenesis.
source: Whereas transcription factors have been well-established critical regulators of neural crest development and craniofacial morphogenesis reviewed in Gou et al., 2015, growing evidence indicates an essential role for post-transcriptional regulation in these processes (Cibi et al., 2019; Copeland and Simoes-Costa, 2020; Dennison et al., 2021; Forman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as recent evidence with citations.
